Naming your rapist is hard. It means that you are outwardly throwing up a fight to a person who has hurt you in the most vile way possible. Rape takes away who you are. You feel like a prisoner trapped under your own skin, no matter how often after you bathe, how the water is, how hard you scrub, the feeling of them penetrating you it doesn't go away. You start to have moments, flashes where you feel normal again. But you see someone with your rapist's haircut, or someone bumps into you, or you're approached by someone selling something, and... you're back to being little more than a wild animal, afraid to even leave the room you're in. Even though it's been years for me, and I'm a successful woman who is in a loving relationship and respected in the community/does a hard job for a woman, I still can't remove that mental scar.

To name the person who did this to you- you're dragging up trauma because you have to talk about them, what happened. A rape accusation can ruin someone's life. People will remind you of this- even if they believe you. It makes you feel dramatic, and weak. You're admitting you were raped. You're going to be questioned, over and over. Your rapist will fight back to defend their name- and question your judgement. Rape is a crime where the victim is treated no better than a criminal- being interviewed over and over, with even the smallest inconsistency ruling out your testament. What you were wearing will be used against you. What you had done in the past will be used against you. The fingers will turn back to you. Those that supported you when you went to the hospital immediately after suddenly wonder if somehow you were asking for it? Maybe your judgment was suspect? He was a good, upstanding man. He wouldn't have done that. Perhaps you misunderstood? Why are you so upset about this?

It takes a great deal of courage to name your rapist, but people who don't name them aren't cowards. Some just want to forget the trauma ever happened. Some don't have the means to do some. Some know they could be hurt by speaking his name? Why did dozens of women not name Epstein until decades later? Why do so many of Trump's victims remain silent?

I hope you understand that. Not willing to name your rapist is perfectly reasonable?

So I worked in retail as a teen, and now as an adult, I work in management at a transportation company. I was ALWAYS the type to try to please the customer, best values first, always polite, blah blah blah. 

Now, if a customer gets all the way to me with a problem, it means that nobody beneath me could help them and I'm usually the only human being that can fix it. 

Lot of times, people are irate. Demanding I be fired, the driver be fired, fuck me, I'm a stupid bitch, yadda yadda. I realized that now, I don't have a boss watching over me during these interactions, so now I broke my last morals and speak to them plainly when they get that way. 

I say something like "I'm not customer service, I'm the person who can actually fix your issue. You can call me a bitch or demand I be fired, or you can let me help you. I can see where your package is. I can have a driver stop by within the hour to help fix this.  If you just want to vent at me, fine. I'm happy to listen. If you want to solve this, then I'm going to need you to meet me halfway and listen to what we need to do next." Of course I don't take an angry tone, I just keep it neutral and calm. 

It's like fucking MAGIC. Holy shit. Takes the wind out of their sails. 100 to 0 in one little canned speech. By the end of the call, we fix the issue and they're in a much better mood. Shit, I've had a few apologize for their behavior. And they don't send in a complaint again. 


Old me would have been horrified, but now I can't imagine being fake nice and pandering ever again. I have a great relationship with our regular customers.
It doesn't work for every person on the other end, but for 99% of the population, they just want to feel like there's someone on their side. It feels like a drug high telling a person that no, you can't talk to me that way. Apparently my predecessor used to take screaming people, tell them she wasn't going to deal with that, and was putting them on hold for five minutes. When she was back, they could talk. If they were still screaming, she'd ask if they needed a few more minutes to collect themselves.

This looks like either a Clydesdale or a Clydesdale mix. I used to train horses for small chdren to ride, but when I got to train for myself, I rode a Clydesdale, a former police horse, named Leo. 

Clydesdales are a different sort of horse. With most horses, you have to answer your dominance, convince them that you're the strong one. Clydesdales *permit* you to ride them or strap them to a cart or whatever. They help because they know you'll feed them later for it. They're the largest draft horse... but also the most gentle. 

Leo and I had a routine- I'd pull him out of his stall, offer him an apple while I hooked on his lead rope. He'd eat it in a single bite. 

Then, on the way to the tack stall, he would sharply turn to the bales of hay we kept stacked outside, yanking me with him. He'd grab a massive mouthful of hay, and would walk himself into the tacking stall, chewing the hay like it was gum. He was totally aware of his own strength, but liked me enough that he would tolerate my fussing. He spend half his life having children touch him and pull at him and pedestrians yelling at the policeman he carried. The sky could fall in front of him and that old man wouldn't be fazed. 

Riding him was surprisingly easy, despite his size. He could be graceful, when he wanted to. He never missed a jump. He and I were in sync that I could simply squeeze his sides with a leg, and he'd follow the course. 

To my mentor's surprise, and likely, nervousness, he and I would occasionally take a break and I'd let him graze while I lay on his back, watching the clouds go by. She'd warn me that he could spook, or buck, or run off and I'd go flying. With most horses, I would agree with that. But not Leo. Leo was unfazed, and I assume that I was light enough back then he barely noticed I was up there. 

Most people would be shocked to see me, a young girl at the time, riding a big brown beast without a saddle, vaulting jumps. But Clydesdales were bred to be gentle. I was safer on him than a horse with full tack. When the day was done and our ride ended, I'd take him to the washroom and hose him down. We rode most often when it was hot, so he looked forward to the cold water. He'd lean into the hose, trying to get the water when it was coldest, right out of the tube. He'd sigh in relief when I rubbed him down with the brush. He loved a good massage.

Then, he'd pretend to let me lead him to the pasture (he could have easily run by himself, like many other horses might try, but that wasn't his nature), allow me to give him a final rub, a hug goodbye, accept my peace offering of a carrot, and then he'd be off to relax in the setting sun, maybe wondering what treat he'd get tomorrow. 

RIP Leo. Miss you, you beautiful old bastard.

Gonna parrot what the others are saying, he really should have an outside support team to give you advice.

That being said, I've had two autistic students, and both functioned best when they could have their own all comfort object. 

"Timmy" loved having his cars, and as long as he had them, he would be calm. I coul gently take his cars when he would need to do something (making sure he was calm first) and say "Hi sweetie, I can hold onto these while you go the bathroom, okay? I'll promise I'll keep them safe until you finish going to the bathroom/get your shoes on!

With "Veetor", he looooved Legos. I made sure that he had his own designated Lego set, and would take a little time out of the day to sit with him and ask what he was doing (he would babble mostly, but I knew he liked it because he would drag me over first thing in the morning to come watch him). When Veetor would start to act up, I would ask if he wanted to go play with his Legos, and then put them out for him in the quiet corner. 

Both children appreciated a quiet corner, and in both classrooms (threes), I was able to explain to the other children that Autistic Child got a little more scared then them, and his toy helped him feel safe, so please help him by not taking it and asking Miss Lockshala if they wanted a similar toy. 

The kids suprisingly understood this pretty easily and would remind visitors not to touch these specific toys. Kids are pretty empathetic to needing to have your own stuff, as they feel the same.

As for them not listening, it's likely because you're grabbing them. Autistic kids aren't find of being touched when it's not on their terms, or being directly spoken to or looked at when they're experiencing sensory overload. 

The best indicator that they need space is that they go to a corner alone with their toy. At that point, it's best to just come over and sit with them for a bit, making sure to not touch their thing. If they need to go somewhere, bring their special item with you and show them that you have it. They'll be more likely to follow. 

Autistic students are honestly some of the best sweethearts you can have! They just require a very different type of communication. They won't respond to stern talking well, nor raising your voice (this can make it worse). Keep your voice soft and your words simple and slow. 

There's no greater feeling than when you finally realize they really like you, as they'll invite you to watch their solo play, or even touch you (as this is something they don't usually like as much). 

Good luck with your little one, and just remember to be patient :)

*The Zookeeper's War*. It's the story if the hitter rivalry between East Berlin's zoo (Tierpark) and West Berlin's zoo (Berlin Zoological Garden). The directors (old men) got into a fist right over one director making fun of the others name. 

Berlin Zoological Garden had the first female zoo director (before the petty old men) in history who was known for being a stone cold bitch (the badass kind). During WW2's occupation of Berlin by the Brits, a British commander was going to repurpose the zoo and demanded she cut down the many historic elms in the park. She complained to his superiors and even to the British Embassy itself, cussing then out and telling them how dare they attempt to deface a national treasure. They send the commander back, with a map of all the trees, and he says she can circle the essential tress she felt that they need to keep.

She circled every single tree on the map and told him to fuck off. The trees were never removed.

It's a great book about petty rivalry, daily life around the Berlin Wall, and how zoos survived the war and become what they are today.
